newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Japan emerging as world's top beef importer - WTO.
newsitem.headline: Japan emerging as world's top beef importer - WTO.

text.p: The outlook is bleak for world beef markets hit by the mad cow scare but booming imports by Japan offer some relief to exporters, a new trade report says.
The report by the Geneva-based World Trade Organisation said Japan replaced the U.S. as the world's top beef importer in 1996 and predicted double-digit growth in Japanese imports.
But it saw no recovery for depressed world beef markets with sharply lower prices and concerns over the mad cow disease.
Panic broke out earlier this year after Britain disclosed the fatal disease -- Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) -- could spread to humans, triggering a public health scare.
The European Union imposed a ban on imports of British beef in March and sales dropped because of the mad cow health scare.
The WTO forecast beef imports by the European Union, where consumption dropped sharply since the outbreak of the mad cow crisis, to fall two percent in 1996 to 450,000 tonnes.
EU intervention stocks, which were virtually zero at the beginning of the year, had begun to build up again, it added.

In sharp contrast, the report forecast a 10 percent jump in Japanese beef imports in 1996 to 1.03 million tonnes, making it the biggest buyer on world markets -- followed by the United States with 1996 imports put at 943,000 tonnes.
The report, "International Markets for Meat 1995-1996", covers production, consumption, trade and prices for beef and veal, pigmeat, poultry meat and sheepmeat.
The WTO predicted a five percent rise in Russian beef imports in 1996 to 440,000 tonnes.
It said the biggest slump in beef imports in 1996 would be in Canada, down 18 percent over 1995 to 210,000 tonnes, and in Brazil, down 16.5 percent to 250,000 tonnes.
Australia remained the world's largest beef exporter in 1996 despite drought with foreign sales expected at 1.08 million tonnes, down one percent over 1995, the report said.

EU was the second top beef exporter in 1996 with a projected one million tonnes and the United States was the third with 962,000 tonnes, up from 826,000 tonnes in 1995, followed by New Zealand, Argentina, Brazil, Canada and Uruguay, the WTO said.
The report said the United States in 1996 was expected to become a net exporter of beef for the first time since 1945 as a result of low domestic prices and favourable exchange rates.

In the Pacific rim, New Zealand had raised its market share in Korea and Japan partly at the expense of Australia. In South America, Argentina suffered from lower sales to its main EU market but was expanding sales to Brazil and Uruguay.
